title: HLock: Harness Portability for Agent Configs
story_key: story|title:hlock harness portability for agent configs
content_excerpt: Your agent is more than a model. It's a harness, MCP servers, skills, and config, hand-tuned on one machine. hlock is the missing harness packaging layer: harness.lock tracks all of its dependencies, so you can commit it to git and restore it anywhere. The harness version, models, MCP servers, skills, plugins, instruction files, and config, each with a digest. Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, autonomous agents like OpenClaw, and more . API keys and tokens become HLOCK_SECRET_* placeholders, so the lock is safe to commit. You supply the values when you sync. hlock sync restores the setup on a new machine, in an isolated directory, or in a Docker image, and tells you exactly what it can't do for you. hlock launch starts your harness in an isolated environment that matches the lock, with none of the unlocked config on your machine. Contributors to one repository rarely share an agent setup: one uses Claude Code with hand-written skills, another uses Codex with a different model. Each person can commit their own lock to .hlock/locks/harness.<handle>.lock , next to the code it was used on. Anyone with a clone can then try a teammate's setup in isolation with hlock launch --lock , or hlock pull it from outside the repository. Add the hlock badge to your README to point readers at the locks. See Team repositories for the layout and the commands. hlock migrate moves a lock onto another harness, Claude Code to Codex say: skills, MCP servers, and instructions go where the new harness reads them, and models move to a provider it supports. hlock localize turns any lock into an equivalent on an open-source harness and models served by a local runtime like Ollama or LM Studio. It's like cross-compiling: your MCP servers, skills, and instructions come along. Give it an eval pack , and it measures the local candidates against your tasks. Some jobs need judgment, not a script. hlock meta hands them to an agent, the meta harness , and checks every result: Use the agent built into hlock, or a harness you already have (Pi, Codex, Goose, OpenCode, Hermes), on your API key or, with --local , open-weight models. It asks before every command, or runs --headless against an allowlist. A locked harness is a baseline. Once your setup is reproducible, you can measure it: every lock hlock resolve writes records its success rate, cost, and latency on your own tasks. The tools will look familiar: Draft an eval pack from the sessions your agent already logged, list the models and harness

title: A zero-dependency auditor for AI agent exposure (secrets, SSH, configs)
story_key: story|title:a zero dependency auditor for ai agent exposure secrets ssh configs
content_excerpt: An AI coding agent runs with your rights. It can read your .env , your SSH keys and your shell history, and run commands. Nothing "malicious" has to be installed for that to go wrong. This page explains why signature antivirus does not cover that, what does, and how to check your own machine in three minutes. The one-minute check (terminal, Node.js installed). Copy each line, press Enter: A classic antivirus compares files and behaviour against known malware. That works when something foreign runs on the machine. With an AI agent the situation is different: the program is legitimate, it is signed, it was installed on purpose, and it acts with your user rights. The risk is not a virus. The risk is what the agent can reach and what can talk it into using it. That is the reasoning behind the product, not a measured detection statistic: if the dangerous thing is a secret lying in a readable file, the useful check is "which secrets lie where, and who can read them", not "does this binary match a signature". This is not theory. In August 2025 the s1ngularity attack on the Nx build tool shipped malware that looked for installed AI command-line assistants and told them to search the victim's file system for credentials, SSH keys and wallets. Weeks later the self-spreading Shai-Hulud npm worm hunted for publishing tokens. Both worked because the secrets were sitting where any process of the user could read them. Dante is a free, open command-line watchman for machines you own: your Mac, Linux or Windows computer, and servers you can reach by SSH. You talk to it in plain German, English or Spanish. It reads, it explains, and it changes nothing without a clear yes. Dante is young. It is a watchman, not a real-time engine: it looks when you ask or on the schedule you agreed to, and it does not scan running processes for malware. What it does well is the boring, high-value part: finding the secrets and settings an attacker or a hijacked agent would use first, and refusing to claim more than it can prove. Its language layer (what you type) is trained on about 259,000 labelled sentences and answers "I don't know" instead of guessing when unsure. You never have to decide everything now. Start with step 1. Dante asks before every next thing, and every question shows the exact command first. Same program, same words, on every system. Not sure where your terminal is? title: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3
story_key: story|title:build specialized multimodal models with lfm3
content_excerpt: LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs. LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B . The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens. Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device. Each model runs in transformers . The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports. Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card . Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. title: How AI agents shape experts’ judgment calls
summary: In a randomized trial, professional analysts working with an AI coding agent went with the option the agent was randomly assigned to favor 86% of the time. We look at what this means for human oversight of AI-assisted work.
story_key: story|title:how ai agents shape experts judgment calls
content_excerpt: When experts hand their work to an AI agent, the usual assumption is that they still make the decisions that matter. The agent writes the code, runs the numbers, and offers advice, but the expert decides what to measure, how to interpret ambiguous evidence, and what the next steps should be. Often there is more than one reasonable answer to these questions, and the decision will come down to the experience and values of whoever makes the call. We wanted to look at whether experts really do make those important decisions, or whether in practice they defer to their AI agents. In a study we report in a new paper , we asked 50 professional analysts to do a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code. They all had experience in causal inference—that is, working out from data whether one thing causes another. Their task was to advise a farming cooperative on whether an advisory service it was running was effective and should be expanded. Along the way, the analysts had to make four choices between two reasonable options, such as whether to measure productivity as crop yield per hectare or as yield per unit of operating cost, and then make a final decision. To see whether they were making these calls themselves, we set up each analyst’s agent to favor one option on each decision, which the analysts weren’t told about. Which way the agents would “lean” would be decided by coin flip. The agent was told to make the best honest case for its lean, to change its mind if the evidence demanded it, and never to mislead. Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%. When analysts had already expressed their own preference before the agent weighed in, they switched away from it 60% of the time if the agent disagreed, compared to 6% if it agreed. Afterward, when asked to explain their choices, 77% of analysts used the agents’ own arguments—sometimes word for word—but only 15% credited the agent as the source of those arguments. Analysts who followed the agents’ recommendations closely were about as confident in their final recommendation as the rest, and roughly as likely to call it the product of their own judgment. We don’t know how much this tells us about the real world. title: Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation
summary: Genie 4: our new world model unlocking unprecedented realism in real-time simulation.
story_key: story|title:genie 4 a new generation of world simulation
content_excerpt: Today, we are announcing Genie 4, our new world model, which unlocks unprecedented realism and improves real-time interactive simulation. Genie 4 is natively multimodal, enabling audio-like music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue to be simultaneously generated with the world. The Genie 4 model incorporates and builds on capabilities from the Gemini family: Gemini Omni anchors the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models provide the complex reasoning needed to help maintain a simulation’s coherence and continuity. With this foundation, you can set an event in motion, and Genie 4 simulates what happens next: how the world responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Understanding and simulating the world is a crucial aspect of building AGI. Genie 4 advances our ability to create safe, infinitely variable simulations that can help with everything from developing training environments for robots and agents to unlocking the creation of new interactive experiences. We have started rolling Genie 4 out as a research preview for trusted testers — gathering feedback before we release it to consumers and developers, starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie here . Genie 4 delivers enhanced photorealism, fluid movement, and native audio. All accompanying sounds featured above are produced directly by Genie 4. The following are recordings of real-time interactions from Genie 4, where users use standard keyboard controls for navigation and camera control, and text prompts to steer the scene as it evolves. With Genie 4, you can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene. Between your inputs, Gemini also monitors and steers the scene to keep the world progressing cohesively. Prompt: Use the reference image as the exact first frame and visual basis for the scene. Preserve the same floating rectangular platform, weathered concrete edges, wild grasses, ferns, twisted small tree, warm glowing amber sphere, and the same middle-aged man in a loose brown suit playing a brass saxophone. title: Interpretable Meta-Policies for Neural Decision Making
summary: Deep Reinforcement Learning remains difficult to interpret and align due to the black-box nature of neural networks. While (neuro-)symbolic approaches improve transparency by incorporating symbolic reasoning, applying them directly to low-level actions results in overly complex, unreadable policies. We introduce NEXUS, a hierarchical RL framework that resolves this tension by combining neural skills with symbolic meta-policies. By shifting transparent reasoning to high-level skills rather than atomic actions, NEXUS drastically reduces symbolic complexity without sacrificing environment performance. Object-centric observations enable high-level reasoning and the design of reward functions and meta-policies by interaction with LLMs. We demonstrate that NEXUS agents learn disentangled skills, are interpretable regarding high-level goals, are better aligned to goals described in the game manual, less prone to reward hacking and more robust to game simplifications than deep RL. Finally, we isolate and evaluate the impact of different meta-policy architectures (neural, symbolic, neuro-symbolic) on environmental return and aligned task performance.

title: How to Build Proactive, Always-On Agents with the Schedules SDK in Managed Deep Agents
summary: Most proactive agents run on a simple cron. Learn what scheduled runs unlock, from memory to smart triage, and how to add them to Managed Deep Agents.
story_key: story|title:how to build proactive always on agents with the schedules sdk in managed deep a
content_excerpt: Ever hear of the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon? It's when you learn a word for the first time, and suddenly start hearing it everywhere. I think the same principle applies in software engineering: You learn about a simple, but effective, design pattern, and then suddenly start seeing it everywhere. We're seeing this happen with proactive agents, where we've noticed that nearly all of your favorite emerging proactive agentic systems are powered by a very simple mechanism: Agent runs as cron tasks, leveraging a more than fifty-year old principle of operating systems for a very modern use case. The future belongs to proactive, always-on, ambient agents. Launches like Muse, Instinct, Dots, Claude Duet, Hone, and more reflect this. Crons power a few different capabilities that combine to make these agents proactive, personalized, and ambient — that is, they can perform tasks on their own, without being manually instructed. In this blog, we will go through the capabilities that crons unlock, the two core underlying parts you need in order to build agents like this, and then show examples of how you can do this in Managed Deep Agents . We’ve seen the impact crons can have. Proactivity is the new default for agent behaviour because of the breadth of new functions it unlocks. More than 70% of Managed Deepagent runs on LangSmith come from scheduled runs rather than a human typing a message. Crons, despite being a simple concept, unlock a few different behaviors that shape these proactive, always-on agents. Memory: A distinctive part of all these agents is that they remember facts about you over longer time horizons. Implementing this partially involves running a background job to condense previous conversations into a denser form of memory. This is colloquially called “dreaming”. Under the hood, this is just a cron that runs on some cadence (e.g. once a day) and updates long-term memory with any learnings from reflecting on the conversations. Proactiveness : Part of what makes these agents work is that they initiate communication about an idea that they think you may be interested in. Under the hood, the way that this works is there is some “idea” of what this agent should be accomplishing. For a general purpose agent, it may be as simple as being a good assistant: taking steps to anticipate what you need next, like flagging an upcoming deadline, following up on an open thread, or surfacing news related to your work. title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
story_key: story|title:can we trust llms to judge whether a research idea is novel
content_excerpt: Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets. At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas. But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work. That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate. Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline. If AI is going to play a larger role in scientific discovery, we need more dependable ways to tell whether it is actually proposing something new. title: How We Built Our Design Agent
summary: How LangChain built Content Studio, an open-source design agent in Slack that makes on-brand videos, graphics and decks, and the harness that powers it.
story_key: story|title:how we built our design agent
content_excerpt: The promo above was made by Content Studio, our design agent that can create videos, social graphics, recreated UI images, slide decks, and more from just a single prompt in Slack. Every asset the agent produces is written in code. Content Studio was built entirely in-house on Managed Deep Agents . It’s now one of the most widely used GTM agents within our company, but it didn’t start out that way. Early feedback was… not great. We've spent four months teaching Content Studio our taste and design principles, mostly by watching it get things wrong in front of the whole company. This post walks through how our GTM Engineering team worked with our design team to build Content Studio from scratch: what good design means to us, how we taught the agent our taste, and the harness that lets it make anything from a still to a launch film. LangChain moves fast. We have constant product launch campaigns, webinars, blogs and events. Each initiative needs assets, from blog headers and diagrams to decks, videos and ad creatives. Our design team was stretched thin, with repetitive requests crowding out more strategic and innovative work. As a lean startup, we needed a low-friction way for anyone at the company to create high-quality, on-brand work. To address these needs, we built Content Studio, a design agent that lives in Slack. A team member describes what they want and attaches accompanying content or briefs, and the agent returns finished, on-brand files. To build Content Studio, we needed three things: Managed Deep Agents gave us everything we needed to productionize Content Studio inside our company: a managed LangSmith Sandbox , integration with Slack, managed tools, scoped agent memory and scheduling agent runs. This allows a small team to spend its time on the design work, the skills, tools and Slack experience, instead of the plumbing. Before jumping into the build, let’s first address the debate of the century: can AI actually produce good design? The model was already good at execution and could write HTML and CSS, chart specs and animation timelines. However, it didn't have our context, so it reached for familiar patterns, what Anthropic calls “distributional convergence” . The result could look polished and still look like a hundred others, or be beautifully animated and never get its point across. Familiar isn’t always bad, but we wanted our agent to make choices that followed its purpose. Katie Dill , Head of Design at Stripe, makes a helpful comparison

  • Fixed the /model and /effort cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.
